item.title: Climate financing falls far short of needs
item.description:
A water pump powered by solar energy serves a slum in Amlapara, Sirajganj town. Since the pump was installed two years ago, residents have faced somewhat less difficulty in accessing water. On a midday in June, several women, including Maksuda Begum and Rahela Khatun, spoke about their experiences there. Rahela said, “Previously, water from the municipal supply line came twice a day. We had to stand in a queue for it. There was no guarantee when it would arrive. Now, we can get water whenever we want.”

The pump was installed through a local NGO initiative funded by a climate fund. However, one pump is far from enough to meet the growing demand. According to locals and municipal officials, there are around 30 slums in the town, but no other slum has a similar facility. In other words, climate financing falls far short of what is needed.

For those who move to towns after losing their homes to floods and river erosion, access to safe drinking water, housing and sanitation remains extremely limited. The experience with the pump in Amlapara shows that even a small project with modest funding can bring significant changes to people's lives. At the same time, a look at the other slums in the town reveals just how limited the available funding is.

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that nearly US$230 billion (approximately Tk 28.52 trillion) will be required by 2050. However, the climate-related allocation for 25 ministries and divisions in the 2026–27 fiscal year stands at Tk 517.46 billion. Of this, the Climate Change Trust Fund, which is financed by the government itself, has received only Tk 1 billion. A large portion of international public climate finance also comes in the form of loans. Despite the increase in funding, the question remains whether it is reaching the people most at risk.

Huge gap between needs and financial flows

Mita Rani Das (52), a marginal farmer from Ashashuni upazila in Satkhira, suffered major losses twice last year. The widow runs her household with income from a small fish enclosure. During an intense heatwave, nearly 30 per cent of the fish in her enclosure died. Later, heavy rainfall in July caused the enclosure to overflow, destroying most of the remaining fish. She received no advance weather warning.

From the coastal areas of Satkhira to the slums of Sirajganj, the impacts of climate change are no longer a future concern. River erosion, salinity, cyclones, excessive rainfall, waterlogging, heatwaves and irregular monsoon patterns are putting people's livelihoods, housing, health and food security at risk every day. Although Bangladesh contributes very little to global carbon emissions, it bears a disproportionate share of the damage.

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that nearly US$230 billion (approximately Tk 28.52 trillion) will be required by 2050. However, the climate-related allocation for 25 ministries and divisions in the 2026–27 fiscal year stands at Tk 517.46 billion. Of this, the Climate Change Trust Fund, which is financed by the government itself, has received only Tk 1 billion.

However, it would be incorrect to attribute every incident of unusual rainfall, heatwaves or river erosion solely to climate change. Natural river dynamics, land use, unplanned urbanisation and weak infrastructure also increase the damage. In many cases, climate change intensifies and increases the frequency of risks, making these longstanding problems even more dangerous. Climate financing plans must therefore take into account not only climate risks but also local environmental conditions and governance weaknesses.

According to the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2023–2050, nearly US$230 billion will be required by 2050 to implement 113 initiatives. An average of US$8.5 billion will be needed annually, of which US$6 billion is expected to come from international funds and development partners.

The NAP identifies eight priority sectors, including water, agriculture, fisheries, transport, urban development, health and disaster management, under six adaptation goals and 23 strategies. This means the estimated funding is not meant solely for embankments or large infrastructure projects. Local early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, safe drinking water, healthcare, livelihoods and support for displaced people moving to cities are also part of the plan. Reaching Mita Rani Das with timely weather alerts or installing more water pumps in Amlapara are therefore also part of the country's national adaptation efforts.

On the other hand, according to Bangladesh's Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDС 3.0), US$116.18 billion will be required to achieve its emissions reduction targets by 2035. Of this amount, US$25.95 billion is expected to be mobilised domestically, while the remaining US$90.23 billion will depend on international financing, technology transfer and capacity-building support.

The figures in the NAP and NDC cannot be added together directly. The NAP primarily estimates the cost of long-term adaptation. The figure in the NDC relates to mitigation, or emissions reduction activities. The two documents also have different timeframes and sectoral coverage. However, both demonstrate that the financial requirements of Bangladesh's climate plans far exceed the capacity of its domestic budget.

Bangladesh’s hidden climate bill: How much are we losing?

Three types of activities must also be distinguished in discussions on climate financing. Mitigation means reducing emissions, such as through renewable energy and energy-efficient technologies. Adaptation means helping people and the economy adjust to risks that have already emerged or are expected to arise. Loss and damage financing is needed when losses cannot be prevented even after adaptation measures have been taken. The loss of land to river erosion or property destroyed by cyclones are examples. Covering up shortfalls in one sector with progress in another cannot provide a true picture of the actual needs.

Climate budget: Figures rise, but questions remain

According to the Finance Division's climate budget report for the 2026–27 fiscal year, the climate-related allocation for 25 ministries and divisions stands at Tk 517.46 billion. This represents 5.52 per cent of the national budget of Tk 9.38 trillion. As a proportion of the combined allocations for the 25 ministries and divisions concerned, the figure is 11.03 per cent, up from 10.07 per cent in the previous fiscal year.

The budget includes initiatives such as afforestation, control of air and plastic pollution, carbon trading, and the ‘One Child, One Tree’ programme. A large portion of climate-related expenditure is spread across ministries responsible for local government, water, agriculture, disaster management and infrastructure. Therefore, looking only at the allocation for the Ministry of Environment does not provide a complete picture of the government's overall climate spending. Similarly, the entire budgets of these ministries cannot be counted as climate expenditure; only the portions identified as such are included in the report.

A large portion of international public climate finance also comes in the form of loans. Despite the increase in funding, the question remains whether it is reaching the people most at risk.

The allocation of Tk 1 billion is a separate matter. It does not represent Bangladesh's entire climate budget, but only the allocation for the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund. The government can use this fund for relatively small and urgent initiatives beyond the large projects undertaken by different ministries. Although the national budget has increased more than eightfold, the annual allocation for the fund, established one and a half decades ago, has not increased proportionately.

Environment and climate expert Haseeb Md Irfanullah told Prothom Alo that this year's budget showed some positive trends in environmental conservation and tackling climate change. However, there are no clear guidelines on where the funding for implementing major goals will come from. In his view, the allocation of Tk 1 billion to the trust fund is disappointing compared with the actual requirements.

The publication of the climate budget report and the identification of expenditure by 25 ministries represent institutional progress. However, questions remain about how effective all the expenditure classified as ‘climate-related’ actually is. Roads, bridges, drainage systems or water projects do not automatically become climate-resilient infrastructure simply because of their classification. Their designs must take climate risks into account, along with beneficiary selection and long-term outcomes.

The link between allocations and results should also be made public. Without indicators showing how many people were protected from waterlogging through the excavation of a canal, how many health centres were made ready to deal with heatwaves or how much the distance to safe drinking water has been reduced in coastal areas, it is impossible to assess the quality of expenditure. It is also essential to determine from the outset where the funding for maintenance will come from after a project is completed. Otherwise, the infrastructure may remain in place, but services could cease after a few years.

National Policy Dialogue brings smallholder farmers’ voices to the centre of climate adaptation policy

A 2025 review by the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) found that the implementation rate of the climate-related development budget had remained at around 85 per cent for several years. CPD Distinguished Fellow Fahmida Khatun, who was involved in the research, told Prothom Alo that the problem was not just the amount allocated but also the quality of expenditure. It is necessary to examine whether the funds are reaching the areas that are most vulnerable to climate change and whether women, children, older people, persons with disabilities, farmers and fishers are at the centre of the projects.

Commitments rise, but adaptation lags behind

According to the latest figures from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), developed countries provided US$132.8 billion in climate finance to developing countries in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024, or helped mobilise funds from private sources. The annual target of US$100 billion, which was supposed to be achieved by 2020, was met for the first time in 2022, two years behind schedule.

Beyond the overall amount, the questions arise on where the money is going and under what conditions. The United Nations Environment Programme's Adaptation Gap Report 2025 says developing countries may need between US$310 billion and US$365 billion annually for adaptation by 2035. However, international public adaptation finance amounted to only US$26 billion in 2023, US$2 billion less than the previous year. The gap between requirements and available funding is 12 to 14 times.

The latest picture of global financial flows reveals the same contrast. According to the Climate Policy Initiative's Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2026, total climate finance exceeded US$2 trillion for the first time in 2024. Of this, US$1.9 trillion went towards mitigation. In contrast, adaptation finance declined in 2023 and remained almost unchanged in 2024. In other words, while investment is increasing in different sectors with sizable markets, such as solar power, electric vehicles and clean energy, funding for safe drinking water, agriculture, health and disaster-resilient livelihoods is not growing at the same pace.

The United Nations Environment Programme's Adaptation Gap Report 2025 says developing countries may need between US$310 billion and US$365 billion annually for adaptation by 2035.

Financing from multilateral development banks is also increasing rapidly. According to the joint figures of 10 major banks, their own climate finance reached approximately US$163 billion in 2025. Of this, US$103 billion went to low- and middle-income economies. Adaptation accounted for US$35 billion. This funding is important for major projects in developing countries. However, since a large portion of financing from development banks comes in the form of loans, the terms and the borrowers' ability to repay them are equally important.

The figures from Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) are not directly comparable. The OECD counts finance provided or mobilised by developed countries; UNEP tracks international public adaptation finance; and CPI presents a picture of global flows combining domestic and international, public and private sources. Failure to understand these differences creates a risk of counting the same funding more than once.

Large portions are loans

One of the major debates on international climate finance is whether assistance should come in the form of grants or loans. The historical responsibility for climate change lies primarily with industrialised countries. Therefore, vulnerable countries argue that it is unfair to impose additional debt burdens on countries that have contributed little to emissions but are struggling to cope with the damage caused by climate change.

According to the OECD, loans accounted for 73 per cent of the public climate finance provided by developed countries in 2023 and 67 per cent in 2024. Grants accounted for 24 per cent and 29 per cent, respectively. However, not all loans have the same terms. Some carry market rates, while others offer lower interest rates and longer repayment periods. Therefore, interest rates, repayment periods, grace periods, currency and whether a project will generate revenue are all important considerations.

International public adaptation finance amounted to only US$26 billion in 2023, US$2 billion less than the previous year. The gap between requirements and available funding is 12 to 14 times.

The problem is that many adaptation projects do not generate direct revenue. Although embankments, canal re-excavation, mangrove restoration, early warning systems and safe housing for poor people offer significant social benefits, their commercial returns are limited. Ultimately, the responsibility for repaying loans for these projects falls on the government budget. Depreciation of the taka can further increase the cost of foreign currency loans.

It is also important to consider where the loans are being used. Projects that save electricity and generate revenue or reduce expenditure may be able to repay loans obtained on favourable terms. However, projects to rehabilitate families who have lost their homes to cyclones or provide safe drinking water in salinity-affected areas have little scope for generating revenue. Grants or long-term financing on highly concessional terms should be prioritised for such initiatives. Otherwise, the burden of climate-related losses ultimately falls on taxpayers in the affected countries.

Process of accessing international funds is complicated

Bangladesh has so far received approval for US$464 million in financing from the global Green Climate Fund (GCF) for a total of 10 projects. However, only one project has been completed so far, for which US$9.7 million was received from the GCF. As a result, Bangladesh has received only a very small portion of the approved funding. An additional US$6.1 million in support has been approved for project preparation and capacity-building. However, the overall size of a project may be larger if other organisations provide co-financing.

This funding is important, but it is limited compared with the annual requirement of US$8.5 billion under the NAP. Moreover, approval, agreement, disbursement and expenditure at the field level are four separate stages. It is difficult to understand the actual progress without the publication of simple and up-to-date official figures showing how much funding has reached each stage. Accessing GCF funding also requires navigating complex proposals, technical capacity requirements, environmental and social safeguards, financial management procedures and lengthy accountability processes.

Therefore, the ability to access international funds does not simply mean being able to write an application. There must be a list of project proposals ready with information on the specific risks in different areas, the amount of investment required, the potential outcomes of each project and how activities will continue after the funding ends. Unless information from ministries, local governments, research institutions and private organisations is brought together, similar small projects are repeatedly undertaken, while proposals for large and integrated initiatives remain undeveloped.

A test case for local financing

The Climate Bridge Fund (CBF) was established in 2019 with support from BRAC and Germany's KfW Development Bank. The fund provides grants to local non-governmental organisations to support people in cities who have been displaced or are at risk of displacement due to climate change.

Bangladesh has so far received approval for US$464 million in financing from the global Green Climate Fund (GCF) for a total of 10 projects. However, only one project has been completed so far, for which US$9.7 million was received from the GCF.

According to the OECD's 2025 review, the CBF had initial capital of approximately US$22 million. By investing in government bonds, it generates an annual income of around US$2 million. This income is used to provide grants for local adaptation projects. As of September 2025, grants had been provided for 26 projects, with an average of less than six months between application and the first disbursement.

The OECD also reported that these projects had provided social and economic support to 15,000 vulnerable households. Water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure had been developed for more than 100,000 people, while 27,000 slum residents had benefited from flood-resilient walkways and drainage systems. The management, financial and technical capacities of 20 grassroots organisations had improved, while more than 200 organisations had received training. However, these are primarily documented results reported by the fund. Independent and long-term evaluations are needed to understand how sustainable these changes are.

This is an alternative way of delivering funding directly to local organisations beyond large international projects. However, the fund should regularly publish information on what will happen to grants if interest income from government bonds declines, how the real value of its capital will be protected amid inflation, and how much people's vulnerability has been reduced after project completion. In addition to rapid disbursement, the fund's success must also be assessed based on its impact several years later.

Md Golam Rabbani, director of the Centre for Climate Change and Environmental Research at BRAC University, told Prothom Alo that new initiatives should be welcomed. However, small initiatives can only go so far; the government must also focus on large-scale financing to address the major climate crisis.

New sources, but not a substitute for grants

Fifteen houses have been built for people who lost their homes to river erosion in the Puthiabari area near the river protection embankment in Sirajganj. Farida Parvin is one of them. After river erosion destroyed her home, she took shelter with her husband and three children in a small room in a slum in the town. She has now moved into a new house with a green tin roof. It has an insulation layer beneath the roof, as well as safe drinking water and a toilet. Compared with her previous home, this one feels like a mansion to her.

The water pump in Amlapara and the houses in Puthiabari offer hope. However, scattered small-scale projects are not enough to meet the needs of hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people. Bangladesh faces three realities simultaneously: risks are increasing, public funding is limited, and international financing is uncertain and conditional.

The invisible cost of climate change: Bangladesh's non-economic losses

Therefore, funding sources such as private investment, green bonds, blended finance, impact investment, carbon markets, disaster risk insurance, local adaptation funds and urban climate finance need to be expanded. However, these are not substitutes for grants. Since adaptation projects offer limited commercial returns, public funds and international grants must be used as catalytic capital to attract private investment where appropriate.

These funding sources also serve different purposes. Green bonds can raise funds for long-term environmentally friendly infrastructure. Under blended finance, public or grant funding takes the first loss, reducing risks for private investors. Insurance can provide rapid financial assistance after disasters, but subsidies are necessary if premiums are beyond the reach of poor people. Carbon markets can generate revenue, but unless reliable emissions reduction accounting, local people's rights to land and resources, transparent verification and fair distribution of revenue are ensured, they could create new disputes.

The role of local governments must also be strengthened. Information on where waterlogging occurs, which settlements face water shortages and who is most vulnerable to heatwaves is most readily available at the local level. However, small municipalities and local organisations have limited capacity to develop projects, manage tenders and accounts, and meet the requirements of international funds. Providing funding alone will not be enough; technical assistance for project preparation, simplified application procedures, and funding for operation and maintenance must also be ensured.

The Finance Division and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) are working on developing Bangladesh's first National Climate Finance Strategy. The Economic Relations Division also has an International Climate Finance Cell. What is now needed is a comprehensive public database in one place, showing domestic allocations, foreign commitments, approvals, loan and grant terms, disbursements, expenditure and outcomes.

Chittagong Hill Tracts: Land disputes, climate change and obstacles to forest conservation

The international assistance landscape is also uncertain. According to preliminary OECD estimates, official development assistance (ODA) from members and partner countries of the Development Assistance Committee fell by 23.1 per cent in real terms in 2025, the largest annual decline on record. Climate finance and development assistance are not the same, but budget cuts in donor countries could also put greater pressure on climate grants. Therefore, it is essential not only to explore new sources of funding but also to ensure that available funds are prioritised and used effectively.

Bangladesh therefore needs three types of measures: consistent and adequate allocations from its own budget, increased grants and concessional financing from international sources, and mechanisms that allow local institutions to access funds directly. Climate risks and outcomes must be measured for every project, and vulnerable people must be involved in planning and monitoring. Otherwise, large figures will remain on paper, while residents of many slums like Amlapara will continue waiting for a single pump providing safe drinking water.

item.title: Rooppur begins 'power start', moves closer to supplying electricity to national grid
item.description:
The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Pabna is conducting the final series of tests before beginning electricity generation. The first unit has successfully completed its nuclear reaction phase. After reviewing the results of the physical tests, the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) has authorised the plant to proceed to the final stage of commissioning. During this stage, the plant will supply a limited amount of electricity to the national grid for the first time.

Sources at the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant said BAERA approved the next stage of work on Thursday afternoon based on the results of the physical tests. This stage is known as the power start or C-stage. Various tests will be conducted to verify the plant’s safe and stable operation.

These will assess the performance of the reactor, cooling systems, turbine, generator, electrical systems and control systems. The reactor’s power level will be gradually increased while these systems are monitored. A major milestone in this stage will be connecting the generator to the national grid, followed by efforts to ensure a stable electricity supply.

The plan was to begin the process of generating energy through nuclear fission at Rooppur in September. However, the schedule was pushed back after a fault was detected during tests of a safety valve. After the problem was successfully addressed, nuclear fission began on 11 October with BAERA’s approval.

Rooppur is the largest single project in Bangladesh’s history. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission, under the Ministry of Science and Technology, is implementing the project. The state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL), under the commission, is responsible for operating the plant. Russian contractor Atomstroyexport is constructing two 1,200-megawatt units at Rooppur.

NPCBL Managing Director Md Zahedul Hasan told Prothom Alo that BAERA had approved the power start, or C-stage, on Thursday afternoon.

“Some tests will be conducted during this stage as well. Power generation will begin at zero. Once the power output rises from zero to 30 per cent, trial electricity supply to the national grid will begin,” he said.

People involved with the project said physical tests are conducted to assess the behaviour of the nuclear reaction inside the reactor vessel. The tests also verify whether all equipment associated with power generation is functioning properly. This is a crucial stage before electricity generation begins. BAERA approval is required before the plant can proceed to each stage.

Sources at Rooppur said the plant would initially generate thermal energy at a limited level, which would then be gradually increased. With the approval of the C-stage, the plant has crossed another major milestone towards connecting to the national grid for the first time. Every stage will be carried out in compliance with the highest safety standards, approved procedures and regulatory requirements.

How electricity will be generated

The process of generating thermal energy will begin with nuclear fuel fission. The heat produced will be used to generate steam, which will drive a turbine to produce electricity.

Once power generation begins inside the reactor vessel, output will be gradually increased. When the plant reaches 30 per cent of its capacity, it will be able to supply electricity to the national grid. At that level, each unit will generate 300 megawatts of electricity. This could happen in December.

Plant officials said trial operations could continue for seven to eight months after the process begins. However, once electricity is supplied to the national grid, Bangladesh will become the world's 33rd country to generate nuclear power.

Rooppur was recognised as a nuclear installation in October 2023, when nuclear fuel arrived at the project site. Bangladesh was also included among countries possessing nuclear power capability following the handover of the fuel.

The Rooppur project was originally scheduled to run until December 2025. Its deadline has since been extended twice, with the latest deadline set for June 2028. Under the contract with the contractor, the project cost cannot be increased despite the extension of the timeline.

However, the rise in the US dollar's exchange rate has increased the project's cost by Tk 260 billion. The total cost of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant is expected to reach Tk 1.39 trillion.

item.title: Spain mourns after latest train tragedy kills 68
item.description:
Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister reported an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.
The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage at night to find further victims on the key line linking Madrid with the southern city of Seville, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, AFP reporters saw.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when "I woke up and I was in the air."
Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling AFP that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.
Wearing a bloodstained grey jumper and holding his tattered suitcase, he recounted "a very strong hit... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos".
"I think I've been born again," he said.
A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones.
Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears, amid crowds of police and journalists from around the world.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said "long and hard hours" were in store because "every person will manage it in their own way.
"We have people who are in shock, who haven't taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.
The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to enable relatives of the victims to provide DNA samples and help identify the missing.
Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims' families.
"What matters most is being with the victims' relatives, that they feel the closeness, because words at a time like this are pointless, but a hug helps," he said.
Recalling how he rushed to the site of the crash, Fernandez said he was confronted with "an image of desolation, despair, uncertainty, death".
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometres (43 miles) of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25 kilometres before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.
The latest disaster comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.

item.description:
The cause of death of retired Bangladesh Air Force (BAF) Flight Lieutenant Tahsif Souri will be known after the completion of the preliminary investigation and autopsy, said Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Thursday.
“Once we receive the post-mortem report and examine all relevant aspects, we will be able to provide further details,” he told reporters after attending a program at the parade ground of Bangladesh Police Academy at Sarda in Rajshahi.
It is not possible to confirm the cause of death before the investigation and autopsy, he said.
Referring to the law and order situation, the minister said the government is successfully identifying and arresting suspects, conducting investigations and ensuring trials after crimes are committed.
However, he acknowledged that there might be exceptions in a few cases.
The minister also claimed that since the BNP assumed office, there have been no extrajudicial killings by law enforcement agencies, bomb attacks or deaths in custody.
Earlier, river police have recovered the body of a former Bangladesh Air Force officer, Tahsif Souri, from the Turag River in Dhaka.
Inspector Firoz Uddin of the River Police’s Tongi outpost told the media on Thursday that they received information through the national emergency service 999 and recovered the floating body from the Rajabari Ghat area of the river around 4:30pm on Wednesday.
“We found a mobile phone with him and identified him through the phone,” he said.
Shahinur Zaman, duty officer at Uttarkhan Police Station, said on Thursday morning that the Tongi River Police outpost recovered the body from the Turag River on Wednesday afternoon.
As the matter fell under the jurisdiction of the River Police, its members went to the spot and took the body away.
Inspector Firoz Uddin said there were no visible injury marks on the body.
The body of Tahsif was sent to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for an autopsy to determine the cause of death.
According to the River Police’s preliminary report, Souri was wearing white pyjamas and a black shirt.
A wristwatch was found on his hand, while an iPhone was found in his pocket.
Souri reportedly recorded the video that circulated on August 5, 2024, showing then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina leaving the country by an aircraft from Kurmitola Airport.

item.title: Shama outlines Bangladesh’s foreign policy vision at Chatham House
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday outlined the government’s strategic vision for strengthening social resilience and promoting sustainable and inclusive growth.
The state minister, while addressing a roundtable discussion hosted by Chatham House, one of the world’s foremost international affairs think tanks, in London also outlined the government’s strategic vision for fostering constructive engagement and friendly relations with all countries, guided by the principles of mutual respect and dignity.
The session brought together scholars, academics and experts from Chatham House and other leading UK research and academic institutions.
The discussion covered a wide range of issues, including Bangladesh’s development priorities, economic diplomacy, business and investment, human rights, youth empowerment, food security, technology-driven economic growth and the creative economy.
Climate resilience, climate finance and priorities ahead of COP31, as well as Bangladesh’s foreign policy approach and engagement with international partners, were also among the key themes.
The state minister elaborated on the Government’s major initiatives, key priorities and foreign policy objectives, underscoring their alignment with the electoral manifesto.
High Commissioner of Bangladesh to the United Kingdom Muhammad Abdul Muhith and senior officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Bangladesh High Commission in London were also present.
The discussion was held under the Chatham House Rule, facilitating an open exchange of perspectives.

item.title: EC secretary: EC satisfied with peaceful Thakurgaon-1 by-election
item.description:
Election Commission (EC) Senior Secretary Akhtar Ahmed on Thursday expressed satisfaction over the peaceful completion of the parliamentary by-election to the Thakurgaon-1 constituency, as no reports of untoward incidents had been received throughout the day.
“We have completed a good election in a peaceful environment with everyone's cooperation,” he said at a post-balloting briefing at the Election Commission Building in the city’s Agargaon area in the afternoon.
The EC secretary said the commission had not received any reports of untoward incidents from anywhere since the morning.
“I believe you also have no such information that could make us concerned,” he said, thanking everyone for their cooperation in holding the election peacefully.
In response to a question about whether the EC was satisfied with the polls, Akhtar Ahmed said: “Surely satisfied. Is there any reason not to be satisfied?”
Asked whether the EC had passed the test set by the 11-party alliance, which had described the by-election as a test for the commission before deciding whether to participate in the upcoming local government elections, he said, “If we had not passed, would we be briefing you?”
He said the voting in the by-election began at 8am and ended at 4pm. All polling stations completed voting, and no voters were waiting to cast their ballots at the end of polling.
The EC secretary said: “Voters exercised their franchise in a festive atmosphere.“
The Thakurgaon-1 constituency, covering Thakurgaon Sadar, Ruhia and Bhulli upazila, fell vacant after Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir assumed office as president.
BNP-nominated candidate Mirza Faisal Amin, who is the younger brother of President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, and Jamaat-e-Islami candidate Delwar Hossain are considered frontrunners in the by-election.
The Thakurgaon-1 constituency has a total of 185 polling stations. Of them, 113 are in Thakurgaon Sadar upazila, 33 in the newly formed Ruhia upazila and 39 in Bhulli upazila.
The constituency has 515,853 voters, including 257,219 men, 258,630 women and four third-gender voters.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,249 as seven die in 24 hours
item.description:
Seven more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Thursday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,249.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all seven of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,144, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 105, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the seven new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with four deaths.
A total of 1,251 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Thursday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 226,357.
During the same period, 64 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,695.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 201,468 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 193,301 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Brac Bank reports stellar performance in Q3 ‘2026
item.description:
Brac Bank delivered a strong set of results across profitability, operating efficiency and balance sheet expansion in the third quarter of 2026, underpinned by well diversified businesses, strength of its governance and customer-focused strategy.
On a consolidated basis, including all subsidiaries, the bank reported a 38% year-on-year increase in Net Profit After Tax (NPAT) to Tk2,121 crore for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared with Tk1,536 crore in the corresponding period of 2025.
On a standalone basis, NPAT rose 50% year-on-year to Tk1,584 crore, up from Tk1,055 crore a year earlier.
Despite a challenging macroeconomic and industry environment, Brac Bank continued to outperform the market, delivering robust balance sheet growth.
Compared with December 2025, customer deposits increased 16%, while loans and advances grew by 7%.
The bank also strengthened operational efficiency, reducing its cost-to-income ratio to 41% at the end of third quarter of 2026, compared with 46% in the corresponding period of 2025, reflecting sustained focus on productivity, cost discipline and digital transformations.
Consolidated Earnings Per Share (EPS) increased to Tk7.70 in Q3 2026 compared to Tk5.29 in the corresponding period of 2025.
The bank’s consolidated net asset value (NAV) per share rose to Tk56.40 on 30 September 2026 from Tk44.84 on 31 December 2025.
Brac Bank’s standalone total customer deposit grew by 16% in September 2026 compared to December 2025, showing strong alignment with its long-term growth strategy and customer confidence.
Consolidated Return on Equity (RoE) and Return on Assets (RoA) stood at 20.28% and 1.65% respectively.
Total consolidated revenue increased by 26% compared to corresponding period of 2025, driven by higher non-funded income coupled with interest income.
The bank’s NPL ratio (non-performing loans) stood at 2.27% in Q3 2026 compared to 2.27% in December 2025.
Regarding Brac Bank’s financial results, managing director and CEO Tareq Refat Ullah Khan commented: “Our third quarter performance reflects the strength of our business model, prudent governance and disciplined execution. Continued customer confidence has enabled us to deliver growth well above the market while maintaining one of the industry's strongest asset quality indicators. We will stay focused on creating sustainable long-term value for our customers, shareholders and the economy.”
As of September 30, 2026, the bank’s customer deposits exceeded Tk103,091 crore, while loans and advances reached Tk77,947 crore, bringing the fund under management to more than Tk181,038 crore.
The bank continued to record balanced growth across its Corporate, SME and Retail Banking segments while maintaining one of the lowest non-performing loan (NPL) ratios in the industry.
Strong balance sheet expansion, improved operating efficiency, most diversified portfolio and disciplined risk management collectively contributed to the bank’s robust earnings performance.
“Our achievements would not have been possible without the trust of our customers, the strategic guidance of our Board of Directors, the support of Bangladesh Bank, and the unwavering commitment of our colleagues. We are strongly committed to sustaining business growth while upholding the highest standards of governance, innovation, transparency and customer service,” Tareq Refat Ullah Khan added.

item.title: Bogra University eyes first student intake in 2026-27
item.description:
Bogra University is preparing to admit its first batch of students in the 2026-27 academic session, ending a 25-year wait for the institution to become operational.
Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Kudarat-e-Jahan announced the plan at a press briefing held at the university’s temporary academic building. He said admissions would begin through the cluster-based system, subject to final approval from the University Grants Commission (UGC).
Bogra University of Science and Technology Act was passed in 2001, but the institution never became operational. A new law, gazetted on July 16 and effective from July 19, has paved the way for its transformation into a full-fledged multidisciplinary university, the vice-chancellor said.
He said the new law differed significantly from the 2001 legislation, delaying preparations for the university’s launch. Academic and administrative preparations had since been completed over the past two and a half months.
The university has recruited 11 staff members on a contractual basis, including four officers and seven employees. Six members have been appointed to its 17-member syndicate. The syndicate and academic council will take final decisions once the required membership is complete, he said.
The temporary campus has smart-board-equipped classrooms, a computer laboratory, safety measures and safe drinking water. A UGC delegation led by members Prof Abdullah Al Mamun and Prof Muniar recently visited the campus to assess its readiness.
The university has proposed nine employment-oriented disciplines, including artificial intelligence, robotics, computer science and financial technology (fintech), for UGC approval. Once approval is secured, student admissions will be started through the scheduled cluster-based admission test in March, the vice-chancellor said.
He also pledged a zero-tolerance policy towards nepotism in teacher recruitment, saying appointments would be based on merit rather than personal connections or recommendations.

item.title: Villagers block highway over proposed new upazila
item.description:
Hundreds of residents of Rammrail Union in Brahmanbaria Sadar blocked the Dhaka-Sylhet highway on Thursday, protesting a proposal to form a new upazila named Barishal by carving out four unions from Brahmanbaria Sadar and Bijoynagar upazilas.
The protest took place at Rammrail Bazar from 11am to noon, with residents from different villages gathering at the local bus stand carrying banners and festoons. They formed a human chain and staged a demonstration, disrupting traffic on the busy highway.
The protesters alleged that district BNP leader and Bhuiyan Foundation Chairman Kabir Ahmed Bhuiyan was behind the proposal to form the new upazila by separating Rammrail, Sultanpur and Basudeb unions from Brahmanbaria Sadar and Singarbil Union from Bijoynagar.
Addressing the gathering, Rammrail Union Jubo Dal General Secretary Shamsuzzaman Sohag said residents would resist any attempt to reorganise the area against their wishes.
“Rammrail is at the heart of Brahmanbaria. The people of Rammrail, Sultanpur and Basudeb have taken to the streets. We will not allow this plan to succeed,” he said.
Young lawyer Mukul Chowdhury said the demonstration was aimed at protesting the proposed formation of a new upazila by bringing together unions from different existing upazilas.
He vowed that the movement would continue until the proposal was withdrawn, adding that residents of the affected unions would resist the move.
In a written statement, local resident Iman Hazari said residents would not accept any proposal to place Rammrail and Sultanpur under an administrative jurisdiction other than Brahmanbaria Sadar.
“Brahmanbaria Sadar is our identity, pride and honour. We will protest any decision imposed on us by disregarding the opinions and interests of local people,” he said.
The protesters also called for an impartial investigation into allegations involving Kabir Ahmed Bhuiyan, including claims that he had used personal connections and influence to pursue various activities. They urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to intervene, saying no individual's influence should take precedence over the rights and interests of local residents.
The villagers warned that they would launch further road and railway blockades if the proposed upazila formation process was not abandoned.
They insisted that the four unions should remain under their existing administrative jurisdictions and vowed to resist any attempt to implement the proposal.
The blockade caused severe traffic congestion on both sides of the highway. A similar protest was also held in Sultanpur Union.

item.title: India slashes cancer drug prices by up to 93%
item.description:
India has announced sharp price reductions for 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines, with prices of some formulations falling by more than 90 per cent, offering potential relief to patients struggling with the high cost of cancer treatment.
The revised maximum retail prices (MRPs), issued by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (Nppa) on October 28, will come into effect on November 9. The decision follows the government’s move to rationalize trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in the public interest.
According to the revised price list, the cost of a 21-capsule pack of one brand of palbociclib, used to treat certain types of breast cancer, has fallen from Rs 40,421.33 to Rs 2,720. The price of a 100mg vial of thiotepa, a chemotherapy drug, has dropped from Rs 80,071.86 to Rs 7,150.33.
Other medicines, including dasatinib, lenvatinib, abiraterone and olaparib, have also seen price reductions. The steepest cuts for selected formulations are reported to reach 93.3%.
The price revisions could ease the financial burden on cancer patients and their families, many of whom face substantial expenses during prolonged treatment. The reductions may also benefit patients from Bangladesh who travel to India for specialized cancer care, although the actual savings will depend on the medicines prescribed and their availability.
However, the price cuts do not extend to all cancer medicines. Several high-cost patented treatments, including Keytruda, Tagrisso, Tecentriq, Darzalex and Imfinzi, remain unchanged in the latest revision. The price of ribociclib, another medicine used to treat breast cancer, has also remained unchanged at Rs 24,435, according to the published list.
The decision has drawn criticism from public health advocates, who argue that reducing trade margins alone will not ensure lasting affordability.
Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India) has called for cost-based price controls, permanent and enforceable limits on trade margins, regular monitoring and independent verification of revised medicine prices.
The organization has questioned the policy’s pricing formula, which permits a 42.8% markup over the price to stockist (PTS), arguing that a lower margin could deliver greater savings to patients. It has also raised concerns about the exclusion of medicines supplied free under patient assistance programs from pricing calculations.
S Srinivasan, co-convenor of the All India Drug Action Network, has similarly argued that the existing price-setting framework can leave expensive medicines unaffordable even after trade margins are reduced. He has called for medicine prices to be determined through a cost-based approach.
The Nppa’s revised list reflects information submitted by pharmaceutical companies up to October 27 and may be updated as manufacturers report their revised prices.
While the latest intervention is expected to make some cancer medicines considerably cheaper, its overall impact will depend on the extent of price reductions across treatments and the effectiveness of future regulatory oversight.
Health advocates maintain that sustainable access to life-saving medicines requires more than one-time price cuts, calling for a pricing system that ensures affordability based on patients’ medical needs rather than their ability to pay.

item.title: Houthis say Saudi strike kills 12 in Yemeni residential area
item.description:
The Iran-backed Houthis said on Thursday that a Saudi strike on a residential area in Yemen’s western Taiz province killed 12 people, as casualties mount in the months since the conflict reignited.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government have exchanged daily attacks since a years-long truce fell apart over the summer. In recent weeks, the group has ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia.
“As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district,” the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group’s Saba news agency.
More than 1,600 people have been killed in Yemen since hostilities resumed, with more than 275,000 displaced, according to United Nations figures.
On Wednesday, at least 14 people were killed in Saudi strikes on a petrol station and market, according to the Houthis, while the group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding civilians.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
The Houthis have in turn reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.
Yemen has been reeling from war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.

item.title: ‘Horrific’ Russian drone strike kills 13 at Ukraine train station
item.description:
A Russian drone slammed into a busy platform at a railway station in Ukraine’s Dnipro on Thursday killing at least 13 people in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a “horrific” attack that demands a response from Kyiv’s allies.
The strike came as Ukraine and Russia strive to uphold a fragile local ceasefire in the ravaged city of Oleshky -- under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have faced months of food, water and medicine shortages.
The truce was holding into its third day, both countries said, with the Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announcing that he had “set out with the Ukrainian delegation towards Oleshky” through Belarus and Russia.
But elsewhere, Moscow continued to pummel Ukraine.
The strike at the Dnipro train station hit a platform “where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing,” Zelensky said.
“Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues,” he added, slamming the attack as “horrific.”
Images released by Ukrainian emergency services showed bodies on the platform, rescuers helping victims to safety and two burnt-out passenger trains with their windows shattered.
Russia has fired drones on trains across Ukraine since the first days of its 2022 invasion -- destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing several railway workers.
In September alone, passengers were evacuated from more than 5,800 Ukrainian train services due to the threat of Russian drone strikes, the national railway operator told AFP.
Ukraine’s vast train network is a vital form of transport in the country, where journeys between east and west can take 24 hours.
Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted three jet-powered drones in a daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defenses and hit the station.
The head of Ukraine Railways, Oleksandr Pertsovsky, said an elevated threat level had been announced.
“But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform,” he said on Facebook.
In the aftermath of the attack, Zelensky refreshed his criticism of a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to ease some sanctions on Russia allowing Moscow to release diesel onto global markets.
“How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating,” he asked.
At least five others were killed across Ukraine in separate Russian attacks, according to local officials.
A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, the head of the city’s military administration, Dmytro Bryzhynsky, said.
A drone also slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several -- including a six-year-old -- the local governor said.
Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks, hitting energy sites around major cities in what Kyiv says is a bid to plunge the country into cold and darkness throughout the winter.
The Kremlin earlier this week vowed not to let up in the overall pace of the war even as the sides prepare to restart stalled talks under US mediation.
Zelensky said on Wednesday it would be a “huge success” if the local ceasefire in Oleshky -- brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump -- allowed for the evacuation of stranded citizens.
Locals caught there have resorted to hunting and eating pigeons in recent months, former residents in touch with those in the city told AFP.
Russia and Ukraine are to meet next month with US envoys to discuss ways to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, with no firm dates set for the talks yet.
Several previous rounds have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.
Russia demands more territory in eastern Ukraine and sweeping military and political restrictions on Kyiv.
Ukraine and its allies say ceding ground to Moscow would be tantamount to a capitulation and leave Kyiv vulnerable to future Russian attacks.

item.title: UN: Afghanistan opium poppy cultivation surges despite Taliban govt ban
item.description:
Opium poppy cultivation in Afghanistan more than quadrupled in 2026 despite a Taliban government ban, the United Nations said Thursday, urging that impoverished farmers needed alternatives to the lucrative crop.
Cultivated areas reached 43,000 hectares (around 106,200 acres), up from 10,000 hectares in 2025, while estimated opium production jumped fivefold from 300 tons to 1,500 tons, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) said in a report.
Long the world’s leading producer of poppies, Afghanistan was overtaken by Myanmar after a 2022 Taliban government ban crushed the trade in the country. But rampant poverty has driven some farmers to return to the trade.
“Without opium, we cannot even afford basic food,” Mohammad, a 22-year-old farmer in Afghanistan’s northeast, told AFP.
Afghanistan’s 2022 crackdown drove cultivated areas down from more than 200,000 hectares to 10,000 hectares in 2025.
Myanmar cultivated 53,000 hectares in 2025, with no 2026 figures available.
The Taliban authorities claim to have destroyed more than 22,000 hectares.
But UNODC said many poppy plots were concealed among cereal crops or behind walls, making them difficult to detect.
Mohammad lives with his parents in Badakhshan which has become Afghanistan’s main opium poppy-growing province.
“The Taliban threaten us and do not allow us to grow opium. We cultivate it with a great deal of fear,” he said, asking only to be identified by his first name.
“I want to buy a car, build a house and get married. Without opium, I cannot achieve these things,” he further explained.
In May, two people were killed in clashes that erupted as Afghan security forces moved to destroy opium poppy fields in Badakhshan.
Another 35-year-old farmer named Mohammad, who ploughs his poppy field with an ox, said: “If we grow wheat, it is not enough to sustain our lives. We are forced to grow poppies to earn a good income.”
Mohammad said that he is threatened by the authorities and sometimes his crops are destroyed but he will continue.
“It is the only way to cover living expenses,” he said.
One hectare of wheat generated just over $770 in 2023, compared with $10,000 for a hectare of poppy, according to UNODC.
“Opium prices slightly decreased from US$ 570 per kilogram in 2025 to US$ 500 per kilogram in 2026, remaining well above pre-ban levels of less than $100 per kilogram,” UNODC said in a press release.
“The fourfold increase in opium poppy cultivation shows the difficulty in sustaining decreases in illicit opium cultivation when poor farmers have no alternatives to feed their families,” said UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma.
The Taliban government acknowledged that the ban was not a “sustainable and long-term solution” without alternative livelihoods and economic support for farmers.
The challenge comes as Afghanistan faces the return of 6.6 million Afghans since 2023, climate disasters, dwindling aid and banking isolation since the Taliban movement returned to power in 2021.
With support from Japan and the European Union, UNODC has funded programs to help farmers find alternatives.
Through the NGO Afghan Aid, Zikrullah, 35, who supports an extended family of 12 in Badakhshan, received improved wheat seeds and fertilizer.
“We’re satisfied, it takes less effort than opium and we’re more at ease,” he told AFP, also asking to be identified only by his first name.
A third farmer named Mohammad, 30, who has converted 80% of his land to wheat, told AFP, that the lack of water in recent years has affected crops other than poppy.
To curb opium production sustainably, alternative crops alone are insufficient, UNODC Country Representative for Afghanistan Polleak Ok Serei told AFP in an interview in Kabul.
“Sustainable alternative livelihood requires more than thinking in terms of alternative crops,” he said.
Farmers “need access to markets, including international markets through trades. They need infrastructure, roads, irrigation, storage.”
UNODC estimated in 2025 that approach would require approximately $500 million, but “only 10 percent” had been funded by donors and the Taliban authorities, according to Ok Serei.
The strategy also takes time, he said.
“Thailand spent 15 years investing in alternative livelihood before starting eradicating,” Ok Serei said.
The problem extends far beyond Afghanistan, he said.
“It truly is an international problem,” Ok Serei added, explaining that Afghan drugs were consumed across other continents.
Afghan opium is the main source of heroin in the European Union, where approximately 850,000 people used opioids in 2024, according to the European Union Drugs Agency.
Addressing the problem requires international cooperation, the UN representative said.
Ok Serei called for a “drug demand reduction strategy, not only in Afghanistan but also outside of Afghanistan.”

item.title: Iran Guards says three tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
item.description:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Thursday that three oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz.
“Over the past 24 hours, three violating oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking mines while attempting to pass through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
The vessels had “switched off all their radar and navigation systems” and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said.
It was not immediately clear when the incidents occurred or which flags the tankers were flying.
Since the outbreak of the war on February 28, Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and gas consumption.
The United States has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran’s armed forces have repeatedly accused US Central Command (Centcom), which oversees US military operations in the region, of encouraging vessels to use a southern corridor near the Omani coast that Tehran considers unauthorized.
“The IRGC Navy states that the unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz is mined, and that vessel owners and crews are responsible for transiting these routes and should not pay attention to Centcom’s delusions on social media,” the statement said.
Earlier on Thursday, the British maritime agency UKMTO said it had received a report of a ship on fire in the strait but gave no details about the cause or any casualties.
It was not immediately clear if it was one of the three ships referred to by the Guards.
The organization also said it had captured a US reconnaissance drone during an operation in the Strait of Hormuz in a separate statement.
“The IRGC Navy announced that its electronic warfare unit had successfully captured a US MQM-170 drone during an offensive operation in the western Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said.

item.title: Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government
item.description:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc on Thursday piled pressure on Israeli Arab leaders over unproven accusations of foreign funding, in a push to neuter parties that made strong gains after an otherwise indecisive election.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, a far-right firebrand with a history of attacks on Palestinians, went so far as to encourage Israel “immediately” to order the arrests of Arab party leaders.
Israel was nearing the completion of ballot-counting from Tuesday’s election in which neither Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot looked able to secure a majority in the parliament known as the Knesset.
A looming threat on the horizon, meanwhile, was the prospect of a return to war with Iran, alongside Israel’s ally the United States, which is holding its own crucial midterms next week.
Israel’s election saw a soaring performance by Israeli Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the country’s creation in 1948, as outrage boiled at calls by ministers such as Ben Gvir to treat the Israeli minority group much as Israel has dealt with Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The Arab parties together have enough votes to take the opposition bloc over the finish line, but Eisenkot has baulked, after relentless attacks by Netanyahu who warned his right-wing Jewish base that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power.
Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, a conservative who heads the Central Election Commission, requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security service into allegations that key Arab party Raam received money from Qatar, the energy-rich Gulf powerbroker that has channels for Hamas.
“The Raamgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel’s elections have been stolen!” Netanyahu’s Likud party said.
Government officials did not offer evidence to back the allegations.
Netanyahu himself has long been under the cloud of allegations related to Qatar after the arrests last year of two of his aides for allegedly receiving payments from the Gulf power.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, for years tacitly supported Qatar funding to Hamas-ruled Gaza, hoping to preserve stability.
That paradigm collapsed on October 7, 2023 when Hamas launched a resistance campaign against Israel, under Netanyahu’s watch.
With nearly 93 percent of the vote counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was at 53 seats and the opposition forces led by Eisenkot had 48 -- both well under the 61 needed to form a government.
The two main Arab formations were on track for an unprecedented 19 seats.
Some observers quickly said that the allegations would help Netanyahu by making the Arab lawmakers even more toxic to Eisenkot.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of one of them, the leftist Arab-majority Joint List, told AFP on Wednesday that he was willing to cooperate with the opposition to bring down Netanyahu but without joining it in a government.
He said the priority was to end “Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government” but noted that the Arab lawmakers disagreed on plenty with Eisenkot, who has largely backed the destruction of Gaza ordered by Netanyahu after the October 7 attack.
In response to the new allegations, Eisenkot said he was receiving updates and promised “utmost vigilance” against election interference.
“On the other hand, we cannot allow political actors to exploit the situation and influence the timing of the inauguration of the 26th Knesset,” he said.
One of Eisenkot’s right-leaning allies, Avigdor Lieberman, called the allegations “dramatic and unprecedented” and urged a swift investigation.
An Israeli police statement said that they would investigate every complaint about election integrity.
Netanyahu, who has led Israel on and off for more than 19 years, is known as a wily political operator.
He also tried on Tuesday to raise allegations of fraud, saying that Arab parties were caught with envelopes of cash and encouraging his base to come out in response.
Police said they arrested three suspects but the election commission called it an isolated local case.
Another factor that could play into the formation is an attack on Iran.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened to strike Iran, with his ally, US President Donald Trump, signalling he is ready to attack after next Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is forecast to lose ground.
Eisenkot has warned the military that Netanyahu has no mandate and that officers must not respond to his “political needs.”
But an attack could raise pressure on Eisenkot to join an emergency unity government, an option he has publicly ruled out, or keep the clock running until Israel can call new elections.
President Isaac Herzog will decide after the publication of the official results which person to task with a first chance of forming a government.

RMG exports increase in Q1’FY27
item.description:
The country's ready-made garment (RMG) exports have increased. However, a major portion of this growth stems from products that have traditionally topped Bangladesh's export list.
In contrast, the export of relatively high-value garments is growing slowly, with exports of certain product categories even declining.
As a result, despite the rise in overall export earnings, little progress has been made in product diversification and increasing the share of high-value garments.
This picture emerged from an analysis of Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data compiled by Mohiuddin Rubel, founder and CEO of Bangladesh Apparel Voice (BAV).
According to the data, during the first quarter (July–September) of the current FY27, RMG exports reached $10.58 billion.
In the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, exports stood at $9.97 billion. Accordingly, exports grew by 6.10% or $608 million.
The analysis by BAV's CEO shows that $573 million of this export growth came from basic apparel—meaning nearly 94% of the total export growth was driven by this category.
During this period, basic apparel exports rose by 7.45% to reach $8.26 billion.
The share of basic garments in total RMG exports also expanded, rising to 78.06% from 77.08% in the first quarter of the previous year.
Among basic apparel, the largest contributors to export growth were trousers/pants, sweaters & cardigans, and t-shirts & vests.
Export earnings from these three product categories increased by $201 million, $178 million, and $104 million, respectively.
Combined, these three items accounted for nearly 80% of total export growth.
Meanwhile, children's wear recorded the highest growth rate at 10.19%, though total exports in this category stood at $300 million.
On the other hand, exports of semi-basic apparel saw only modest growth.
This category includes shirts and blouses.
In the first quarter, exports of these items grew by 1.77% to $842 million. Their share in total exports dropped from 8.30% last year to 7.96%.
The picture for high-value apparel is even weaker. Exports of high-end garments increased by just 1.42%, reaching $1.48 billion—a mere $21 million increase over the previous year.
Outerwear exports (coats, jackets, blazers, and overcoats) increased by just $33 million, while technical apparel grew by $18 million.
However, exports of gown-type apparel (frocks, long gowns, or one-piece women's wear) fell by 10.66%, sportswear & activewear dropped by 11.24%, and suits & ensembles declined by 14.48%.
Consequently, the share of high-end garments in total RMG exports contracted from 14.63% to 13.98%.

item.title: Bangladesh’s LDC graduation postponed by 3 years to November 2029
item.description:
Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category has been postponed by another three years. Instead of 24 November 2026, the country will now graduate in November 2029. This gives Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare.

The decision was approved at a plenary meeting of the United Nations General Assembly, which began at 1:00 am today, Friday. The meeting was chaired by UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman. UN Web TV broadcast the meeting live.

At the beginning of the meeting, Uruguay’s representative, speaking on behalf of the G-77, tabled a draft proposal to defer the LDC graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal by three years. No country’s representative opposed the proposal.

Representatives of France, Canada and Ireland, the latter speaking on behalf of the European Union, expressed support for postponing the graduation of Bangladesh and Nepal. However, all of them called for reforms in Bangladesh in their statements.

Bangladesh’s preparations for LDC graduation weak: UN report
Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

On 21 July, the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) recommended that the UN General Assembly take the final decision on Bangladesh’s request for an extension of its preparatory period for LDC greaduation.

Earlier, after reviewing Bangladesh’s application, the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) had recommended that the request by Bangladesh and Nepal to extend their preparatory periods be placed before the General Assembly for consideration. Based on that recommendation, ECOSOC decided to refer the matter to the General Assembly.

The final decision to extend the LDC preparatory period was taken today.

Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from the list of least developed countries on 24 November 2026. Following graduation, Bangladesh would become a fully-fledged developing country.

The United Nations divides its member states into two categories: developed and developing countries. Countries on the LDC list are also developing countries. Those that lag behind other developing countries and require assistance from other nations are classified as least developed countries.

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Why the request for postponement

The policy of remaining firm on Bangladesh’s graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category in 2026 continued till the tenure of the interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus. However, after the BNP government took office in February this year, Bangladesh formally applied for a three-year postponement of its graduation from the LDC list.

The government argued that an extension would provide the necessary policy space to stabilise the macroeconomy, consolidate ongoing reforms, and complete priority activities under the Smooth Transition Strategy (STS).

Bangladesh’s letter also stated that the five-year preparatory period for LDC graduation had been ‘severely disrupted’ by a series of domestic and international crises.

Global crises included the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, a slow global economic recovery, the Russia-Ukraine war and the resulting volatility in energy and food markets, tighter global financial conditions, delays in the recovery of trade, instability in the Middle East and growing uncertainty in the global trading system.

Domestic challenges included irregularities in the financial sector, the political transition following the mass uprising of 2024, and the unresolved repatriation of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.

LDC graduation: What needs to be done after applying for an extension

Bangladesh’s position

Bangladesh was included in the list of least developed countries (LDCs) in 1975. As an LDC, it has since enjoyed various benefits, including duty-free access for its exports. The United Nations Committee for Development Policy (CDP) makes recommendations on which countries should graduate from the LDC category.

LDCs are assessed every three years. A country’s eligibility for graduation is determined on the basis of three indicators: per capita income, human assets, and climate and economic vulnerability. A country must meet the thresholds for any two of the three indicators, or its per capita income must be twice the required threshold. These criteria, however, change over time.

Bangladesh met the thresholds for all three indicators in the 2018 and 2021 triennial reviews. These are gross national income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI) and the Economic Vulnerability Index (EVI).

In 2021, the CDP made its final recommendation that Bangladesh graduate from the LDC category in 2024. However, the graduation was deferred by two years because of the Covid-19 pandemic; otherwise, Bangladesh would have graduated two years earlier. Now, a further three years have been added to the preparatory period for graduation.
